benchmarks.name: Rick's Free Auto Repair Advice
benchmarks.note: independent mechanic's example of a dealer estimate for two front end links on a 2014 Subaru Outback: 2 genuine links at $68 each plus 1 hour at $185/hr, total $321; also gives a general figure of 'about $100 to $150 each'. Page dated 2021

finding: The live range of $100-$575 is about right at the bottom and a little high at the top for links alone; the top only makes sense because the same line also covers bar bushings and dealer pricing. Built totals for both front links, parts + stated hours x $120-$160/hr (the national middle labor rate used for these checks): economy 2015 Corolla about $98-$413 (0.5-1.0 hr); midsize 2016 Outback about $84-$293 (0.3-1.0 hr); truck 2016 F-150 4x4 about $110-$337 (0.5-1.0 hr); luxury 2015 BMW 328i about $142-$320 (0.7-1.0 hr). The bottom: the lowest totals ($84-$142) pair online aftermarket links with a manufacturer warranty time, RepairPal's average is $131-$185 and Jerry starts at $75, so $100 is a fair floor. The top: nothing we can build for a pair of front links passes about $415, and that needs two genuine Toyota links at $126 each; Jerry puts both sides at $200-$300 and a dealer example for an Outback comes to $321. $575 is reached only at dealer labor rates well above $160/hr, with all four links, with seized hardware, or when the job is the bar bushings instead. Bushings: the one stated figure found is a parts seller's 'approximately 2 hours' for a $27.89 front bushing kit on the 2015-2020 F-150, which builds to about $268-$348; Jerry gives $100-$250 where access is easy and 2-4 or more hours where it is not, and on some cars the bushings are bonded to the bar, so the whole bar is replaced (a Tesla bulletin allows 4.35-4.45 for that on the Model S and X). So for links only a range of about $100-$425 fits the evidence, and $575 is defensible as long as the line keeps covering bushings. How solid the labor times are: midsize is the strongest, a Subaru warranty time for the Outback itself (0.3 for both links, 0.2 for one); economy is a Kia warranty time for an Optima (0.5 hr for both), not a Corolla; truck uses a parts seller's 30-minute and 1-hour figures for F-150s, not a book time, with a GM figure for a Colorado (0.6 hr) as a cross-check; luxury is the weakest, a Tesla time for the Model S (0.70), not a BMW. The 1.0 hr high end in three classes is a single dealer estimate for a 2014 Outback quoted by an independent mechanic, who himself calls it a half-hour job. Warranty times are the low end of what shops bill, most shops have a minimum charge of half an hour to an hour, and rusted link nuts that have to be cut off are the usual reason this job runs over. Two parts figures rest on a reading of the listing: the Delphi Corolla kit is counted as one link, and the Ford OEM price is counted per link.
extras: A quote often adds the sway bar (stabilizer bar) bushings and their brackets or bolts, which is a separate and usually longer job; the rear pair of links on cars that have them; new nuts (genuine links are often sold without them); and extra labor for rusted link nuts that must be cut off (one mechanic's guide puts that at around $75-$100). Shops replace links in pairs, so a price for one link is roughly half the parts and a little over half the labor. Also common: a suspension noise diagnosis or inspection fee, since a clunk blamed on links can turn out to be struts, strut mounts, ball joints or control arm bushings; shop supplies and sales tax. A wheel alignment is not normally needed for links or bushings alone.
